# Tubulointerstitial diseases

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Tubulointerstitial diseases > Tubulointerstitial diseases*

[Original Article Link](/library/Jg0sw2)

---

## Summary

Tubulointerstitial diseases are conditions of inflammation of the renal tubules and <u>interstitium</u> that can lead to <u>renal failure</u>. <u>Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis</u> (<u>ATIN</u>) is the third most common cause of <u>acute kidney injury</u> (<u>AKI</u>) in hospitalized patients after <u>acute tubular necrosis</u> (<u>ATN</u>) and <u>prerenal AKI</u>, and it is most commonly caused by an <u>allergic reaction</u> to medications. <u>ATIN</u> commonly manifests with a slowly progressive, nonoliguric, <u>intrinsic AKI</u>. The classic triad of <u>fever</u>, <u>morbilliform</u> <u>rash</u>, and <u>eosinophilia</u> is seen in < 10% of cases. Laboratory study findings may suggest <u>interstitial</u> nephritis, but histological confirmation with <u>renal biopsy</u> is required for a definitive diagnosis. Early recognition, removal, or treatment of the suspected cause, and, in select cases, administration of <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy, will result in complete or partial resolution for most patients, while a minority of patients experience irreversible <u>kidney</u> damage. <u>Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis</u> (<u>CTIN</u>) is commonly due to the progression of <u>ATIN</u>, but it may also be caused by medications, infections, toxins, or systemic diseases. Treatment involves managing or eliminating the underlying cause and <u>management of CKD</u>. Crystal-induced nephropathy is a type of <u>kidney</u> damage that results from crystal deposition in the renal vasculature, the renal tubules, or the draining <u>urinary tract</u> and that may lead to <u>crystal-induced AKI</u>, crystal-induced <u>CKD</u>, or <u>urolithiasis</u>. <u>Renal papillary necrosis</u>, a <u>necrosis</u> of the <u>renal medullary pyramids</u> and <u>papillae</u>, is caused by <u>ischemia</u> (due to, e.g., <u>sickle cell disease</u> and <u>sickle cell trait</u>, acute <u>pyelonephritis</u>, or obstruction of the <u>urinary tract</u>). Patients often present with <u>AKI</u> with <u>hematuria</u> and sloughed <u>papillae</u>. Management should include treatment of the underlying cause, <u>IV fluids</u> to prevent blood clot formation and <u>upper urinary tract obstruction</u>, and management of further complications.

---

## Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis

### Definition




<u>Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis</u> (<u>ATIN</u>) is an <u>acute inflammation</u> of the <u>renal interstitium</u> and tubules that causes a decline in renal function over a period of days to weeks. [[1]](/library/KYXUJ9)




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Third most common cause of <u>AKI</u> in hospitalized patients [[2]](/library/S_cynU0)

* Seen in ∼ 15% of <u>biopsy</u> samples obtained for unexplained <u>AKI</u> [[3]](/library/T_c6nU0)





### Pathophysiology




* Immune-mediated tubulointerstitial damage (allergic interstitial nephritis) is the most widely accepted theory.

* Inflammatory infiltrates → tissue <u>edema</u> and tubular cell damage → compromised tubular flow

* <u>Allergic interstitial nephritis</u>: drugs act as <u>haptens</u> → <u>type IV hypersensitivity reaction</u>  [[4]](/library/6YXjJ9)

* Acute obstruction: crystals (from e.g., <u>uric acid</u>, medications) or <u>proteins</u> (e.g., <u>light chains</u>) obstruct tubules





### Etiology [[1]](/library/KYXUJ9)[[5]](/library/kIYm1q)[[6]](/library/e_cxMU0)




* Medications (most common) [[2]](/library/S_cynU0)

* <u>Antibiotics</u>: <u>β-lactams</u>, <u>sulfonamides</u>, <u>rifampin</u>, <u>fluoroquinolones</u>

* <u>NSAIDs</u>

* <u>Proton pump inhibitors</u> and <u>H<sub>2</sub> blockers</u>

* <u>Loop diuretics</u> and <u>thiazides</u>

* <u>Anticonvulsants</u>: <u>phenytoin</u>, <u>valproate</u>, <u>carbamazepine</u>, <u>phenobarbital</u>

* Other: <u>allopurinol</u>, <u>immune checkpoint inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>nivolumab</u>, <u>pembrolizumab</u>), <u>mesalamine</u>

* Infection

* Bacteria

* <u>Escherichia coli</u>, <u>Brucella</u> spp., <u>Campylobacter</u> spp., <u>Salmonella</u> spp., <u>Streptococcus</u> spp., <u>Staphylococcus</u> spp., <u>Legionella</u> spp.

* <u>Spirochetes</u> (e.g., <u>Leptospira</u>, <u>Treponema pallidum</u>)

* <u>Mycobacteria</u>, <u>mycoplasma</u>

* <u>Viruses</u>: <u>HIV</u>, <u>CMV</u>, <u>EBV</u>, <u>HSV</u>, <u>measles</u>, <u>mumps</u>, <u>hantavirus</u>

* Other

* <u>Parasites</u> (e.g., <u>Toxoplasma</u>, <u>Leishmania</u>)

* Fungi (e.g., <u>Histoplasma</u>, <u>Coccidioides</u>)

* Autoimmune: <u>Sjogren syndrome</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>SLE</u>, tubulointerstitial nephritis with <u>uveitis</u>, <u>IgG4-related systemic disease</u>  [[7]](/library/aX1Q920)

* Other: <u>autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease</u>





> [!NOTE]
> “Please RSVP:” Rifampin, Sulfa drugs and the V (5) Ps (Proton pump inhibitors, Pain killers (<u>NSAIDs</u>), “Pee pills” (<u>diuretics</u>), Penicillins, and Phenytoin) are the drugs that cause <u>acute tubulointerstitial nephritis</u>.




### Clinical features [[2]](/library/S_cynU0)



* <u>Clinical features of acute kidney injury</u>, with or without:

* <u>Morbilliform</u> <u>rash</u>

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Arthralgias</u>

* Flank <u>pain</u>




> [!TIP]
> The classic triad of <u>fever</u>, <u>morbilliform</u> <u>rash</u>, and <u>eosinophilia</u> is present in < 10% of patients with <u>ATIN</u>, but their presence can help to guide the diagnosis. [[2]](/library/S_cynU0)[[6]](/library/e_cxMU0)




### Diagnostics [[8]](/library/b9bHND)[[9]](/library/0_ce5U0)




#### Approach




* Determine if the patient fulfills <u>diagnostic criteria for AKI</u>.

* Obtain a minimum diagnostic workup for patients with suspected <u>kidney</u> diseases.

* Blood tests and urine studies

* Renal imaging studies

* Identify characteristic clinical features, <u>risk factors</u>, and potential exposures for <u>ATIN</u>.

* Consider <u>renal biopsy</u> (<u>gold standard test</u>) if there is no improvement under <u>supportive care</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>ATIN</u> typically manifests as slowly progressive, nonoliguric, <u>intrinsic AKI</u>. However, patients with severe disease may present with <u>oliguria</u> and the course may be rapidly progressive. [[4]](/library/6YXjJ9)




#### Blood tests [[2]](/library/S_cynU0)[[3]](/library/T_c6nU0)[[6]](/library/e_cxMU0)




* <u>BMP</u>: : ↑ <u>BUN</u> and <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>CBC</u>: : ↑ <u>eosinophils</u> (more common in drug-induced <u>ATIN</u>)





#### Urine studies [[2]](/library/S_cynU0)[[3]](/library/T_c6nU0)[[6]](/library/e_cxMU0)




* <u>Urinalysis</u>

* <u>Sterile pyuria</u>

* Subnephrotic-range <u>proteinuria</u>

* Microscopic <u>hematuria</u>

* Urine microscopy

* Up to 20% of patients have <u>bland urine sediment</u>.

* <u>WBC casts</u> , <u>RBC casts</u> , <u>waxy casts</u> , <u>granular casts</u> , tubular <u>epithelial</u> casts

* Urine <u>eosinophils</u> (low <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u> for <u>ATIN</u>)  [[10]](/library/h_ccLU0)

* Urine chemistries in tubulointerstitial disease (findings depend on the major site of injury)  [[3]](/library/T_c6nU0)[[11]](/library/Lybwfw)

* Medullary defects: e.g., urine concentrating defects (<u>nephrogenic diabetes insipidus</u>), <u>sodium</u> wasting

* <u>Proximal</u> tubular defects: e.g., <u>glycosuria</u>, phosphaturia, <u>bicarbonaturia</u>, <u>natriuresis</u>, findings of <u>type 2 renal tubular acidosis</u>

* <u>Distal</u> tubular defects: e.g., <u>natriuresis</u>, <u>hyperkalemia</u>, findings of <u>type 1 renal tubular acidosis</u>





> [!TIP]
> Although frequently cited as a diagnostic clue, in clinical practice, urine <u>eosinophils</u> lack <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u> for reliably confirming <u>ATIN</u>. [[12]](/library/Gg1B9T0)

#### <u>Renal ultrasound</u> [[5]](/library/kIYm1q)




* Indication: to rule out other causes of <u>AKI</u>

* Findings

* Often normal

* May demonstrate enlarged <u>kidneys</u> with <u>increased echogenicity</u>, reflecting <u>interstitial</u> <u>edema</u>  [[3]](/library/T_c6nU0)





![Edematous renal parenchyma with hypoechoic medullary pyramids](media/ngtoro821rl80vfqtwk1092x.jpg)

Edematous renal parenchyma with hypoechoic medullary pyramids




#### <u>Renal biopsy</u> [[6]](/library/e_cxMU0)[[13]](/library/a_cQ5U0)




* Indications include:

* No improvement or the patient worsens after 3–5 days of <u>supportive care</u> and withdrawal of potential causative agent.

* Guiding treatment of suspected causes

* Findings

* Diffuse or patchy peritubular inflammatory cell infiltrates: <u>T-cell</u> <u>lymphocytes</u> and <u>monocytes</u> (<u>macrophages</u>, <u>eosinophils</u>, and <u>plasma cells</u>)

* <u>Interstitial</u> <u>edema</u>

* Sparing of <u>glomeruli</u> and vessels





### Differential diagnoses [[5]](/library/kIYm1q)




* Other causes of <u>intrinsic AKI</u>

* <u>Crystalline nephropathy</u>

* <u>Acute tubular necrosis</u>

* <u>Vasculitis</u>

* <u>Atheroembolic disease</u>

* <u>Glomerulonephritis</u>

* <u>DRESS syndrome</u>

* <u>Prerenal AKI</u>

* <u>Postrenal AKI</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>ATIN</u>, <u>atheroembolic disease</u>, <u>vasculitis</u>, and <u>DRESS syndrome</u> can all manifest with <u>AKI</u>, <u>skin</u> lesions (e.g., <u>livedo reticularis</u>, <u>purpura</u>, or <u>rash</u>), and <u>eosinophilia</u>, and should be considered as differential diagnoses. [[6]](/library/e_cxMU0)




### Management [[1]](/library/KYXUJ9)[[8]](/library/b9bHND)[[13]](/library/a_cQ5U0)




* Stop causative agents or treat underlying systemic disease.

* Provide <u>supportive care for AKI</u>;  for 3–5 days.

* Consider <u>systemic glucocorticoids</u> under specialist guidance.

* Monitor <u>kidney function</u>; evaluate for <u>indications for acute dialysis</u>.





#### <u>Glucocorticoid</u> therapy [[6]](/library/e_cxMU0)[[14]](/library/hzccsU0)




* Common indications

* Specific <u>ATIN</u> etiologies, e.g.:

* Drug-induced <u>AIN</u>

* Autoimmune disorders

* Postinfectious <u>ATIN</u> with delayed recovery

* Insufficient improvement in <u>eGFR</u> after 3–5 days of <u>supportive care for AKI</u>

* Impending <u>indication for dialysis</u>

* Diffuse infiltrates and no extensive <u>fibrosis</u> on <u>biopsy</u> sample

* Example regimen (<u>off-label</u>) : <u>methylprednisolone</u> DOSAGE followed by <u>prednisone</u> DOSAGE [[14]](/library/hzccsU0)

* Important considerations

* There is a paucity of high-quality evidence to support the use of <u>glucocorticoids</u> in <u>ATIN</u>.

* When indicated, <u>glucocorticoids</u> should be started within 7 days of diagnosis.  [[6]](/library/e_cxMU0)[[14]](/library/hzccsU0)

* Consider stopping <u>glucocorticoids</u> if there is no improvement in renal function after 1 week of therapy.

## Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis

### Definition




<u>Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis</u> (<u>CTIN</u>) is a condition of <u>chronic inflammation</u> of the renal tubules and <u>interstitium</u> and can progress to <u>end-stage renal disease</u> (<u>ESRD</u>) after months or years. [[15]](/library/BbXzD9)




### Pathophysiology [[11]](/library/Lybwfw)




* <u>Interstitial</u> <u>mononuclear cell</u> infiltration → tubulointerstitial <u>fibrosis</u> and <u>atrophy</u> → <u>glomerular</u> and vascular <u>fibrosis</u> and <u>sclerosis</u> → chronic <u>kidney</u> damage

* Pathophysiology of specific causes of <u>CTIN</u> includes:

* Progression of <u>ATIN</u>: chronic inflammation → <u>fibrosis</u> → chronic renal damage

* Analgesic nephropathy (e.g., resulting from <u>NSAID</u> use)

* Inhibition of <u>prostacyclin</u> synthesis → <u>vasoconstriction</u> of the medullary blood vessels → <u>papillary</u> <u>ischemia</u> and <u>papillary necrosis</u> [[16]](/library/ybXdw9)

* Associated with an increased risk of <u>urothelial carcinoma</u>; can progress to <u>ESRD</u> [[16]](/library/ybXdw9)

* <u>Reflux nephropathy</u>: chronic high-pressure reflux and recurrent <u>UTIs</u> → tubular <u>atrophy</u> and patchy <u>interstitial</u> <u>fibrosis</u> [[5]](/library/kIYm1q)

* <u>Myeloma cast nephropathy</u>: Excessive amounts of <u>light chains</u> are produced and filtered into the primary urine → precipitation of <u>light chains</u> in renal tubules → tubular obstruction





### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[11]](/library/Lybwfw)




* The overall <u>prevalence</u> of <u>CTIN</u> is unknown.

* <u>Chronic interstitial nephritis</u> in agricultural communities (CINAC) : [[17]](/library/gzcFHU0)

* <u>CTIN</u> with secondary <u>glomerulosclerosis</u>; primarily seen in young male agricultural workers

* <u>Prevalence</u> approaches <u>epidemic</u> <u>proportions</u> (15%) in Sri Lanka, some countries in Central America, and other countries with a tropical climate.





### Etiology [[5]](/library/kIYm1q)




* Medications

* <u>Analgesic nephropathy</u>; : <u>combination analgesics</u> , <u>NSAIDs</u>, and <u>acetaminophen</u>

* <u>Calcineurin inhibitors</u>: <u>cyclosporine</u>, <u>tacrolimus</u>

* <u>Chemotherapeutic agents</u>: <u>cisplatin</u>, <u>ifosfamide</u>

* <u>Nucleoside</u> inhibitors: <u>cidofovir</u>, <u>tenofovir</u>

* Aristolochic acid: causative agent in aristolochic acid nephropathy

* Other: <u>mesalamine</u>, <u>lithium</u>

* Toxins: lead;  (i.e., chronic lead nephropathy), <u>cadmium</u>

* Infections: <u>chronic pyelonephritis</u>, <u>tuberculosis</u>

* Systemic diseases: <u>multiple myeloma</u>, <u>Sjogren syndrome</u>, <u>SLE</u>, <u>sickle cell disease</u>, <u>vasculitis</u>, <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>lymphoma</u>, <u>IgG4-related systemic disease</u>, tubulointerstitial nephritis with <u>uveitis</u>

* Metabolic diseases: <u>hyperuricemia</u>, <u>hypercalcemia</u>, <u>hyperoxaluria</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>

* Miscellaneous

* Radiation nephritis

* <u>Kidney</u> <u>graft rejection</u>

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Ischemia</u>

* CINAC





### Clinical features [[5]](/library/kIYm1q)[[9]](/library/0_ce5U0)




<u>CTIN</u> typically follows an indolent course. Clinical features vary according to the etiology.




* <u>Painless hematuria</u>, <u>pyuria</u>, <u>oliguria</u>, or <u>polyuria</u>

* Colicky flank <u>pain</u>

* <u>Uremia</u> or other <u>symptoms of chronic kidney disease</u>

* Symptoms of an underlying condition (e.g., symptoms of <u>multiple myeloma</u>)

* <u>Type II RTA</u> with <u>Fanconi syndrome</u> resulting from defects in <u>proximal</u> tubules

* <u>Type IV RTA</u> resulting from defects in <u>distal</u> tubules





> [!TIP]
> <u>Analgesic nephropathy</u> increases the risk of <u>urothelial carcinoma</u> and can progress to <u>ESRD</u>. [[16]](/library/ybXdw9)




### Diagnostics [[5]](/library/kIYm1q)[[9]](/library/0_ce5U0)[[18]](/library/LTcwrb0)




Perform a <u>diagnostic workup for CKD</u> and evaluate for <u>risk factors</u> and exposures that suggest <u>CTIN</u> (see “Etiology”).




* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* Obtain <u>BMP</u>, <u>CBC</u>, <u>urinalysis</u>, urine microscopy, and urine chemistries for all patients.

* Findings

* Blood tests: ↑ <u>BUN</u> and <u>creatinine</u>, ↓ <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>  or ↑ <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>; <u>normal anion gap</u> ; <u>anemia of CKD</u> [[2]](/library/S_cynU0)[[3]](/library/T_c6nU0)

* <u>Urine chemistries in tubulointerstitial diseases</u> (findings similar to <u>ATIN</u>): <u>sterile pyuria</u>, <u>proteinuria</u>, <u>hematuria</u>; , <u>RBC casts</u>, <u>WBC casts</u> [[2]](/library/S_cynU0)[[3]](/library/T_c6nU0)[[6]](/library/e_cxMU0)

* <u>Renal ultrasound</u> [[9]](/library/0_ce5U0)

* Obtain to rule out other <u>causes of CKD</u> (not used to confirm or exclude the diagnosis of <u>CTIN</u>).

* Findings

* Typically, small <u>kidneys</u> with <u>increased echogenicity</u>

* Normal to large echogenic <u>kidneys</u> may be seen in infiltrative tubulointerstitial diseases (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>lymphoma</u>).

* <u>Renal biopsy</u> [[6]](/library/e_cxMU0)[[9]](/library/0_ce5U0)

* Can be used to diagnose specific causes that would alter management or help determine the prognosis

* Findings include tubulointerstitial <u>fibrosis</u> and tubular <u>atrophy</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Laboratory findings in <u>chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis</u> have significant overlap with other <u>causes of CKD</u> and are neither sensitive nor specific.




### Differential diagnoses




See “<u>Etiology of chronic kidney disease</u>.”




### Treatment [[18]](/library/LTcwrb0)




Treatment consists of <u>management of CKD</u>, including treatment of the underlying cause.

---

## Crystalline nephropathies

* Definition: : a type of <u>kidney injury</u> that is triggered by crystal deposition and may lead to <u>crystal-induced AKI</u>, crystal-induced <u>CKD</u>, or <u>urolithiasis</u>

* Pathophysiology

* Precipitation of <u>minerals</u> (crystallization) → <u>phagocytosis</u> of crystals → activation of the <u>inflammasome</u> → renal damage

* Precipitation of <u>minerals</u> (crystallization) → obstruction of tubules → renal damage





| <br>Overview of crystalline nephropathies [[19]](/library/pYXLJ9)[[20]](/library/1X12C20)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Renovascular <u>crystallopathy</u> | Tubular <u>crystallopathy</u> | <u>Urolithiasis</u> |
| Pathophysiology | <br><br>* Crystal deposits in the renal vasculature → <u>ischemic</u> renal <u>necrosis</u><br><br>* Stenotic <u>atherosclerosis</u> of renal <u>arteries</u> → renal <u>atrophy</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Crystal deposits → necroinflammation, tubular obstruction, or formation of <u>granulomas</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Crystal deposits in the draining urinary tract → obstruction-related <u>nephron</u> <u>death</u><br><br>* See also “<u>Nephrolithiasis</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| Etiology | <br><br>* <u>Cholesterol crystal embolism</u><br><br>* <u>Atherosclerosis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Drug-induced: e.g., <u>acyclovir</u>, <u>indinavir</u>, <u>ciprofloxacin</u>, <u>methotrexate</u><br><br>* Diet-induced: e.g., diets rich in oxalate, <u>sodium</u>, fructose, <u>vitamin C</u>, <u>sucrose</u>, or low in <u>potassium</u> or <u>calcium</u><br><br>* <u>Hyperuricemia</u> or <u>hyperuricosuria</u><br><br>* <u>Short bowel syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Congenital kidney anomalies</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br><br>* <u>Tumor lysis syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Rhabdomyolysis</u><br><br>* <u>Multiple myeloma</u><br><br>* <u>Hyperbilirubinemia</u><br><br>* <u>Cryoglobulinemia</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Enteric oxalosis</u><br><br> |  |  |
| Clinical features | <br>* Features of <u>AKI</u> or <u>CKD</u><br><br> |  | <br>* <u>Renal colic</u><br><br> |
| Diagnostics | <br>* Crystals may be seen on urine microscopy.<br><br> |  |  |
| Management | <br><br>* Management of the underlying cause<br><br>* <u>Supportive care</u> (e.g., <u>fluid therapy</u>, <u>pain management</u> for colic, <u>nutritional support</u>)<br><br>* <u>Management of AKI</u>, <u>management of CKD</u>, or <u>management of nephrolithiasis</u> (if present)<br><br><br> |  |  |

## Renal papillary necrosis

### Definition




<u>Renal papillary necrosis</u> is <u>ischemic</u>, <u>coagulative necrosis</u> of the <u>renal medullary pyramids</u> and <u>papillae</u> and is a feature of various conditions.




### Pathophysiology




* <u>Ischemia</u> → <u>necrosis</u> and sloughing of the <u>papillae</u> → ureteral obstruction → possible scarring

* Usually bilateral; can also affect a single <u>papilla</u> [[21]](/library/oa10l20)





![Renal papillary necrosis](media/zxk08wu1zy8jg5ow45fls76n.jpg)

Renal papillary necrosis




### Etiology




* Often multifactorial

* <u>Sickle cell disease</u> and <u>sickle cell trait</u>

* Acute <u>pyelonephritis</u>

* Obstruction of the <u>urinary tract</u>

* <u>Tuberculosis</u>

* <u>Cirrhosis</u> of the <u>liver</u>

* <u>NSAIDs</u> (due to inhibition of <u>prostaglandin</u>-mediated <u>vasodilation</u> in the vasa recta)

* <u>Renal transplant</u> rejection

* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u>

* Systemic <u>vasculitis</u>





> [!NOTE]
> POSTCARDS: Pyelonephritis, Obstruction, Sickle cell disease, Tuberculosis, Cirrhosis, Analgesics (<u>NSAIDs</u>), Renal <u>transplant rejection</u>, Diabetes mellitus, and Systemic <u>vasculitis</u> are the causes of <u>renal papillary necrosis</u>.




### Clinical features




* Acute

* Flank <u>pain</u>, colicky <u>pain</u>

* <u>Hematuria</u> (microscopic or macroscopic)

* <u>Proteinuria</u>

* <u>Fever</u>, chills

* <u>Acute kidney injury</u>

* Chronic: : usually asymptomatic or mild symptoms





### Diagnostics [[11]](/library/Lybwfw)[[22]](/library/_bX5w9)




Consider <u>renal papillary necrosis</u> as part of the differential diagnosis for patients presenting with <u>hematuria</u>, particularly if <u>risk factors</u> are present (e.g., <u>sickle cell disease</u>, <u>diabetes</u>, chronic <u>oral analgesic</u> use).




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




* <u>BMP</u>: ↑ <u>BUN</u> and <u>creatinine</u>

* Urine studies [[23]](/library/wX1hZf0)[[24]](/library/9X1NZf0)

* Gross or <u>microscopic hematuria</u>

* <u>Proteinuria</u>

* <u>Sterile pyuria</u>

* Sloughed <u>papillae</u>





#### Imaging studies [[21]](/library/oa10l20)[[22]](/library/_bX5w9)




Obtain in all patients to assess for <u>ischemic</u> changes and exclude differential diagnoses or precipitating conditions (e.g., <u>kidney</u> tumors, <u>pyelonephritis</u>, <u>nephrolithiasis</u>).




* <u>CT urography</u> [[21]](/library/oa10l20)[[22]](/library/_bX5w9)[[25]](/library/yX1d0f0)

* Test of choice for <u>renal papillary necrosis</u>

* Can visualize early <u>ischemic</u> changes (while they may still be reversible)

* Useful for differential diagnosis

* Findings (during the contrast excretory phase) [[26]](/library/BX1zZf0)

* Small, contrast-enhancing <u>papillary</u> cavities abutting the calices

* Filling defects in the <u>renal pelvis</u> due to irregular (e.g., <u>necrotic</u> or peripherally calcified) <u>papillae</u>

* Small <u>kidneys</u> in chronic nephritis

* <u>Renal ultrasound</u> [[21]](/library/oa10l20)

* Quick, noninvasive initial test to assess for <u>hydronephrosis</u>, tumors, or calculi

* Findings: <u>increased echogenicity</u> of the inner medulla; filling defect in the medullary tip (late finding)

* <u>Intravenous urography</u> [[22]](/library/_bX5w9)

* Historically considered the test of choice; <u>CT urography</u> is now preferred.

* Findings: may be normal initially; see findings of <u>CT urography</u> above.





### Treatment [[11]](/library/Lybwfw)




* Treat the underlying cause: See “Etiology.”

* Prevent blood clot formation: Provide <u>IV fluid therapy</u> to maintain high urine output.

* Manage complications if present.

* <u>Management of AKI</u>: e.g., <u>supportive care for AKI</u>; consider <u>indications for acute dialysis</u>.

* <u>Treatment of pyelonephritis</u>: e.g., <u>antibiotic therapy</u>

* Treatment of <u>upper urinary tract obstruction</u>: e.g., <u>ureteral stenting</u>

* Management of <u>massive hemorrhage</u> (rare), e.g.:

* <u>Type and screen</u> and <u>pRBC transfusion</u> as indicated

* In refractory or severe cases: radiographic or percutaneous embolization, or surgical <u>nephrectomy</u>
